stories.title: NASA-funded Study Details One of Oldest Mars Meteorites Ever Found
stories.summary: Scientists age-dated the Teghaza 001 meteorite, finding it formed over 4.1 billion years ago, making it one of the oldest Martian meteorites. Its unique mineralogy provides a rare snapshot of Mars' ancient crust and suggests early interactions between water and rock, matching observations from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.

Its unique mineralogy provides a rare snapshot of Mars' ancient crust and suggests early interactions between water and rock, matching observations from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.
stories.significance: This meteorite offers a "Rosetta Stone" for Mars, providing direct evidence of the planet's early geological history and the interaction of water and rock. Future studies of Teghaza 001 could help answer critical questions about the ancient Martian water cycle and the planet's atmospheric evolution.

stories.title: New dwarf planet candidate discovered by NSF–DOE Rubin Observatory
stories.summary: Scientists using the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory have identified a large object, provisionally designated ED138, orbiting beyond Pluto. Preliminary analysis suggests it may be one of the largest dwarf planet candidates ever found, potentially joining the five other known dwarf planets if confirmed by follow-up observations.

stories.significance: If confirmed, ED138 would join the five other known dwarf planets, expanding our understanding of the solar system's composition and the objects residing in its distant regions. stories.caveat: The object ED138 is currently a "dwarf planet candidate" and its classification is preliminary. Further observations by other observatories are needed to confirm its nature and status as a dwarf planet.

stories.title: NASA’s Perseverance Offers Clues to Protect Crews From Mars Dust
stories.summary: NASA's Perseverance rover measured fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles clinging to spacesuit materials over 1,645 Martian days. The study found that static electricity influences particle adhesion, with organic polymers collecting fine dust. These findings could inform future spacesuit and habitat designs, dust-removal procedures, and crew health standards for Mars missions.
stories.finding: NASA's Perseverance rover measured fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles clinging to spacesuit materials over 1,645 Martian days. These findings could inform future spacesuit and habitat designs, dust-removal procedures, and crew health standards for Mars missions.
stories.significance: These findings are crucial for designing future spacesuits and habitats, developing effective dust-removal procedures, and establishing crew health standards for human missions to Mars. Understanding how different materials attract and retain dust, especially ultrafine particles that can penetrate the lungs and bloodstream, will help protect astronauts from potential health hazards and equipment degradation.

inputFacts.title: NASA’s Perseverance Offers Clues to Protect Crews From Mars Dust
inputFacts.summary: NASA's Perseverance Mars rover measured fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles clinging to spacesuit materials over 1,645 Martian days. The study found that organic polymers, common in spacesuit outer layers, readily collect fine dust, and that the finest particles (down to 100 nanometers) remained attached through years of driving and drilling. The dust is chemically rich in iron, sulfur, phosphorus, and calcium sulfate, and contains chemically reactive compounds like perchlorates and reactive iron.

The dust is chemically rich in iron, sulfur, phosphorus, and calcium sulfate, and contains chemically reactive compounds like perchlorates and reactive iron.

editorial.reason: The article presents new, direct measurements of fine and ultrafine Martian dust, which is a significant hazard for future human missions. The findings have direct implications for engineering and health protocols for space exploration.
editorial.groundingReason: The article fully supports all claims in the summary, detailing the measurements of fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles on spacesuit materials over 1,645 Martian days, the influence of static electricity, and the collection of fine dust by organic polymers. It also explains how these findings will inform future mission designs and health standards. This represents a new finding regarding Martian dust characteristics and their implications for human exploration.

inputFacts.title: Chimpanzees at war: U-M researcher finds hope for humanity
inputFacts.summary: Chimpanzees from the Ngogo community in Kibale National Park, Uganda, split into two groups in January 2018 after a period of increasing aggression, leading to the killing of 28 individuals from one splinter group by members of the other. This lethal intergroup aggression occurred between individuals who had previously spent their entire lives together, affiliated, and cooperated.

inputFacts.title: Stars brewing in a nebulous cauldron
inputFacts.summary: Astronomers detected extremely dim stars less than a tenth as massive as the Sun and distinguished larger, hotter, fully evolved stars from young stellar objects still wrapped in thick clouds within the N159 star-forming region in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Their results showed that the western region of N159 has more young stellar objects in a more concentrated area, indicating it is at an earlier stage of collapsing to form stars.

inputFacts.title: TB 26-09 Measured Hammer-Tap Inputs
inputFacts.summary: An instrumented hammer test does not require an idealized single half-sine waveform for valid results, provided that the complete force and response are measured accurately. inputFacts.title: Five U-M researchers named American Physical Society fellows
inputFacts.summary: Five University of Michigan researchers were elected as fellows of the American Physical Society for their contributions to physics. Scott Baalrud was recognized for advancements in the kinetic theory of plasmas. Emanuel Gull was recognized for advances in numerical methods for strongly correlated electron systems. Cagliyan Kurdak was recognized for leadership in broadening participation in physics graduate education. Venkat Raman was recognized for insights and computational methods for rotating detonation engines. Dominika Zgid was recognized for contributions to ab initio many-body methods for molecules and solids.

inputFacts.title: APOD: 2026 November 1 – Colors of the Moon
inputFacts.summary: The apparent color of the Moon, as observed from Earth, varies depending on atmospheric conditions and the Moon's position relative to the horizon. A collection of full moon images over 10 years from Italy shows that red or yellow hues typically occur when the Moon is near the horizon due to blue light scattering, while a blue Moon is rarer and may indicate larger atmospheric dust particles. A purple Moon's cause is unclear, possibly a combination of effects.

inputFacts.title: Slice of Martian Meteorite Teghaza 001
inputFacts.summary: A slice of the Martian meteorite Teghaza 001, one of the most ancient Martian meteorites found on Earth, was used to determine the age of the rock.
